title: Stop Doing Nordic curl Wrong: Train Your hamstring tendons Instead
description: Kneel tall, anchor your heels, and lower your whole body toward the floor like a falling tree. Your lowering time is the test: how long your hamstring tendons can brake the fall. Most guys train it in a way that teaches everything except the brake. Here is the fix.

scenes.narration: Kneel tall on something soft, with your heels anchored under a couch, a bar, or a partner's hands. Your body is one straight line from your knees to your head. Now lean forward from the knees, keeping that line, and lower yourself toward the floor as slowly as you possibly can, resisting with the backs of your thighs the whole way down. Start your clock when you start to lean and stop it when your hands catch the floor. That lowering time is your number. Keep it. Most people train this movement in a way that skips the only part that matters, and by the end you will know exactly which part that is.

scenes.label: OF CONTROLLED LOWERING IS THE LINE
scenes.sub: under 2: the brake is missing - 6+: full nordic in reach
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Four seconds of controlled lowering, body straight from knees to head, hands catching the floor only at the end, is certified hamstring tendon leverage. Under two seconds, the brake is essentially missing: gravity is doing the lowering and your hamstrings are passengers. Over six seconds, you are most of the way to a full Nordic curl, one of the rarest strength feats a bodyweight athlete can own. Be honest about the middle of the descent, because that is where this test is graded. Almost everyone can survive the first twenty degrees, leaning while the price is low. The test is the range from forty degrees to the floor, where the lever gets long and the brake either exists or does not. Your number is not how the descent starts. It is whether the middle is a controlled burn or a collapse with good intentions.

Look at the back of the knee. Your hamstrings cross two joints, hip and knee, and in the Nordic they work as a brake: lengthening under tension while your bodyweight tries to fold you at the knees. This is eccentric strength, force produced while the muscle stretches, and it is the tendons' favorite language. The hamstring tendons at the back of your knee absorb the load of your entire falling body, multiplied by a lever that grows longer with every degree you lean. At twenty degrees of lean the brake holds a manageable price. At fifty degrees the same brake is holding several times that price, with no change in your bodyweight at all. That is leverage doing what leverage does. The Nordic is not really a leg exercise. It is a brake inspection, and the inspector is gravity, and gravity does not accept excuses.

Here is why this brake matters beyond one exercise. Hamstring injuries are the most common injury in sprinting sports, and they happen in exactly the position the Nordic trains: the leg swinging forward, the hamstring lengthening under load to brake the shin before foot strike. Training programs built around Nordic lowering have been studied for years, and the consistent finding is that athletes who build this eccentric brake suffer far fewer hamstring injuries. The mechanism is not mysterious. A tendon and muscle that have practiced absorbing force at long lengths do not panic when a sprint asks for the same thing at full speed. Compare the two descents one more time. The collapse teaches your nervous system that the middle range is a free fall. The controlled lower teaches it that the middle range is owned. Sprinting will ask which lesson you learned, at thirty kilometers an hour, with no warning. One more detail separates brakes that transfer from brakes that only test well: speed. The Nordic builds the brake slowly, but sprinting spends it in milliseconds, so as your lowering time grows, add faster hinge work, like snap-downs or light, sharp hip hinges, to teach the brake to fire at the speed the road demands. Slow work builds the tissue. Fast work teaches the timing. The sprint will ask for both, in that order, and it will not accept an essay about either one.

The drill that builds the brake at a fair price is the partial Nordic. Set a stack of cushions or a bench in front of your knees at a height that lets you lower under control for the full descent, hands catching at the bottom. Lower slowly, push back up with your hands as much as you need, and raise the target's distance, not your ego, week by week: lower target, longer brake. Two sets of three, twice a week, is a full program for the first two months. The brake grows at the range you train it, so spend your reps in the middle, where the test is graded.

beats.text: LOWER THE TARGET, NOT THE STANDARD

scenes.narration: Your advantage in the Nordic is the same arithmetic as everywhere in this season, with a twist. The falling load is your bodyweight, so the light guy's brake is priced lower at every angle, which means more quality reps before failure and faster recovery between sessions. The twist is that hamstring tendons do not care how you look. This is invisible strength, the kind that never shows in a photograph and decides who is still sprinting at full speed in the last ten minutes of a game. Big quads photograph well. Brakes win races and prevent injuries, and brakes are built from tendon, patience, and exactly your bodyweight. The skinny guy who owns a five-second Nordic lower owns something most of the gym cannot buy at any size: a posterior chain that can absorb force as well as produce it.
Kneel tall with me, heels anchored, body one line. Lower for as many of these thirty seconds as the brake allows, reset, and go again. Slow is the exercise. Go.

Here is the fix. Stop breaking at the hips. The moment your hips fold, the lever shortens, the price collapses, and you have trained a sit-up variation instead of a brake; if you cannot keep the line, raise your target and lower to that. Stop bouncing off your hands and springing back up. The way down is the exercise; the way up is a reset, and pushing up with your arms is not cheating, it is the design. Stop doing these daily. Eccentric tendon work is expensive tissue work, and twice a week with full recovery beats five sloppy sessions that leave your hamstrings permanently half-braked. And stop skipping the warm-up: two minutes of leg swings and easy hinges before the first rep, because a cold brake grabs instead of gripping. The weekly shape: two sessions, partial Nordics to a target, every rep through the middle range under control. The brake you are building is measured in seconds and paid in patience.

beats.text: THE WAY DOWN IS THE EXERCISE

scenes.narration: So, your time. Under two seconds: the brake is missing, and partial Nordics to a high target are your starting line. Two to four seconds: the brake exists and is learning its trade in the middle range. Over four seconds of true control: your hamstring tendon leverage is certified, and the full Nordic curl is a season away, not a fantasy. Retest in thirty days, same anchor, same camera angle, and grade the middle of the descent, not the start. Put your seconds in the comments. Just the number. Gravity grades this test and gravity keeps perfect records. Give it a better number to record.

beats.text: UNDER 2 SEC: THE BRAKE IS MISSING

scenes.narration: Anyone can fall. A trained brake decides how. That is the Nordic, and your hamstrings are trainable. Subscribe, and bring me your new time in thirty days. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
